summary: Lets an OSPF router signal that it requires a working BFD session before an adjacency forms. If both neighbors advertise strict mode, the adjacency is held back until BFD is up, avoiding traffic being sent over a link that is not really working. It updates RFC 2328.

plainLanguage.summary: Two neighbors agree not to start talking until they have both checked the phone line really works.

how does ospf wait for bfd before adjacency
what is the ospf lls b-bit
subtitle: Lets two OSPF routers agree to wait for a working BFD session before they form an adjacency.

tldr.problem: On a degraded link, OSPF can bring up an adjacency that BFD, with its more aggressive timers, then brings down again, which causes adjacency flaps and routing churn.
tldr.mechanism: A router sets the B-bit in the Link-Local Signaling (LLS) block of its Hello and Database Description packets. If both neighbors set it, each holds the neighbor in Init state until a BFD session is up.
tldr.outcome: Adjacencies form only over links where BFD works, while routers that do not support strict-mode still interoperate. The RFC updates RFC 2328.

facts.label: B-bit position
facts.value: 0x00000010 in LLS Type 1 Extended Options and Flags

today: RFC 9355 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2023. It updates RFC 2328, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Flapping Adjacency Problem
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) lets routers monitor data plane connectivity and detect faults in the path between them. OSPF uses it to notice failures faster than the OSPF Hello dead timer allows. Normally the BFD session is bootstrapped from neighbor addresses learned from OSPF Hello packets.

On a degraded, poor-quality link with intermittent packet drops, OSPF may still establish an adjacency while a BFD session fails to establish or flaps. Traffic over the link suffers drops, and OSPF brings the adjacency up only for BFD to bring it down again.

The fix is to block the adjacency until BFD is established, but only when both neighbors ask for it, so routers without BFD still work. The RFC calls this strict-mode. It also applies to adjacency over virtual links using BFD multi-hop, and a similar function for IS-IS is in RFC 6213.
sections.plainLanguage: If a phone line crackles, two friends keep starting a call and losing it. Strict-mode says to test the line first and only then start talking.

sections.title: The B-bit and the IPv4 Address TLV
sections.content:
The RFC defines the B-bit in the LLS Type 1 Extended Options and Flags. It appears in the LLS block of Hello and Database Description packets and indicates that BFD is enabled on the link and that the router requests strict-mode. A router MUST include the LLS block with the B-bit set in its Hello and DD packets when strict-mode is enabled on the link. IANA assigned it bit position 0x00000010.

It also defines the Local Interface IPv4 Address TLV for OSPFv3 IPv4 address family instances. Its Type is 21, its Length is 4 octets, and its value is the primary IPv4 address of the local interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The B-bit is a little flag in each hello that says: I would like to test the line first. The extra address note tells a neighbor where to test.

sections.title: Changes to the Neighbor State Machine
sections.content:
When a router supporting strict-mode finds a neighbor that also supports it, the router establishes a BFD session first and only then brings up the OSPF adjacency. This updates the neighbor state machine in RFC 2328: in strict-mode, the Init state requests BFD session establishment, and a neighbor in Init or higher is listed in Hello packets only if it has a BFD session or did not advertise strict-mode.

OSPF requests removal of the BFD session when the neighbor goes to Down, and requests establishment again on entering Init. An implementation MUST NOT wait for BFD in Init unless the operator enabled strict-mode on the interface and the neighbor signaled it. Otherwise it SHOULD start BFD only in 2-Way or greater state. This lets one router use strict-mode on some interfaces or neighbors and normal mode on others.

After the state machine moves beyond Init, later changes to the B-bit MUST NOT trigger any change to the adjacency or the BFD session. If BFD is enabled where an adjacency is already up with a strict-mode neighbor, an implementation SHOULD NOT bring it down to Init.
sections.plainLanguage: A router waits at the front door, Init, until the line test passes before it lets the neighbor in. If the neighbor is already inside, it does not kick them out to run the test.

sections.title: OSPFv3 IPv4 and Graceful Restart
sections.content:
OSPFv3 with IPv4 address families sends Hellos from an IPv6 link-local address, so a router would only learn its neighbor's IPv4 link address later, from the Link-LSA. Strict-mode needs that address in Init state, so implementations MUST include the Local Interface IPv4 Address TLV whenever they set the B-bit. A receiver MUST ignore the B-bit when the TLV is missing from OSPFv3 IPv4 AF Hellos.

Strict-mode delays adjacency formation, which may affect or break graceful restart recovery. The RFC RECOMMENDS setting graceful restart timers to allow for normal BFD session establishment delays.
sections.plainLanguage: The router needs to know which door to knock on for the test. The extra address note tells it, and without that note the flag is ignored.

sections.title: Compatibility and Operations
sections.content:
An implementation MUST still form adjacencies with neighbors that do not advertise strict-mode, whether they lack BFD or support BFD without strict-mode. A router that does not support the RFC ignores the B-bit, so behavior is the same as before. Implementations MAY offer a local option to force strict-mode only, in which case adjacency with a non-strict neighbor would not form, or an option to enable BFD without strict-mode.

Implementations SHOULD report BFD session status along with the Init state and log neighbor transitions including BFD events, so an operator can spot an adjacency stuck waiting for BFD. Hold-down and dampening can further reduce adjacency flaps, but their details are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers that do not know the new rule just carry on as before, and nobody is locked out unless the owner asks for that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of OSPF Link-Local Signaling (RFC 5613) also apply. Inappropriate use of the B-bit in a Hello could prevent an adjacency from forming or cause a failure to detect bidirectional forwarding failures. If authentication is used in the OSPF routing domain, the Cryptographic Authentication TLV MUST also be used to protect the LLS block contents.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger fakes the flag, neighbors could be stopped from meeting. Signing the messages stops that.
